paragraphs: I've worked in Lamorinda long enough to know that a two-home compound on a hillside acre in Lafayette doesn't come along often, and 1603 Reliez Valley Road caught my attention the moment it listed. The combination of a refreshed main home with four balconies and valley views alongside what sounds like a genuinely architectural ADU believed to be designed by Leon Meyer is the kind of offering that serious buyers remember. When the listing came off the market after 105 days without a sale, I wanted to reach out because I don't think the property was the problem.

What the listing history suggests to me is a strategy gap, not a value gap. At $545 per square foot, the home was priced meaningfully below the Lafayette range for a renovated property with this footprint and setting, which should have been an advantage. Instead, the pricing story was never told in a way that gave buyers the context to understand what they were getting. The ADU alone, with its redwood walls, walls of windows, and independent address, is a lifestyle asset that most buyers have never encountered. That story deserved its own spotlight, not a footnote.

I've put together a short packet that walks through the three friction points I believe kept qualified buyers from connecting with this property, along with a positioning analysis and a framework for how I'd approach a relaunch differently. It's meant to give you something concrete to look at, not a sales pitch.
If you're already working with an agent toward a new listing, please feel free to set this aside. If you're not, I'd enjoy a conversation at whatever pace makes sense for you.

exec_summary.headline: A Rare Lafayette Hillside Compound with Architectural Character  -  and a Listing That Didn't Show It
exec_summary.p1: 1603 Reliez Valley Road is genuinely uncommon inventory for Lafayette. A 4,314 square foot two-home compound on a full acre of hillside, with a refreshed 2,654 square foot main residence featuring vaulted ceilings, hardwood floors, four balconies, and expansive views, paired with a 1,660 square foot ADU believed to have been designed by architect Leon Meyer. The ADU isn't a converted garage. It's a three-bedroom, two-bath retreat with walls of windows, oiled redwood, a remodeled primary suite, and its own address and parking. Buyers who are looking for multigenerational living, rental income potential, or a private creative or work space don't find something like this often in Lafayette. The Sport Court, EV charger, outdoor BBQ and entertaining area, and the hillside privacy round out a property with real lifestyle depth.
exec_summary.p2: The listing spent 105 days on the market and came off without a sale. That outcome doesn't reflect the fundamentals of the property. At $545 per square foot, the compound was priced well below the Lafayette renovated benchmark of $780 to $840 per square foot, which should have generated strong buyer interest. The gap between value and outcome points to a strategy problem: the marketing never built the case for what this property actually is. A two-home compound requires a different narrative and a different buyer than a single-family listing, and a standard approach to distribution leaves that buyer pool largely untouched.
exec_summary.p3: A relaunch needs to lead with the compound story, not bury it. The right buyers for this property are actively looking for something they can't find in conventional inventory, and they need to be found where they're actually searching, not waited for in a standard MLS queue.

forensics.title: Friction #1: 105 Days Without a Pivot
forensics.body: After 105 days on the market, buyer psychology had long since shifted. Past the 45-day mark, buyers stop asking whether a home is worth looking at and start asking what's wrong with it. That doubt wasn't earned by the property. A two-home compound on a hillside acre with architectural ADU and valley views is exactly what a subset of Lafayette buyers has been waiting to find. The listing ran its course without a visible change in strategy, which meant it never had a fresh start with a new audience. The clock ran out before the right buyer was ever genuinely reached.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork's off-market private buyer list at offmarket.brightworkrealty.com gives a relaunched property a clean reset with buyers who are actively opted in to receive property alerts before anything reappears on Zillow, bypassing the stale-listing stigma entirely.

forensics.title: Friction #2: The ADU Story Was Never the Headline
forensics.body: The Leon Meyer-attributed ADU is the property's most distinctive asset, and it needed its own marketing moment. A 1,660 square foot retreat with oiled redwood, walls of windows, a remodeled primary suite with an impressive closet, a built-in office, and a private patio is not a footnote. It's a lifestyle category of its own, whether a buyer is thinking about multigenerational living, rental income, a guest house, or a private studio. When that story lives in the middle of a long listing description without visual depth to back it up, buyers who would have made the drive to see it never got the prompt to do so. The compound format has a specific buyer, and that buyer needed to be shown the ADU, not told about it.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: A 3D Matterport tour of both structures, navigable independently, gives buyers the spatial experience of the ADU before they ever set foot on the property, which is exactly the kind of visual proof that turns a browser into a scheduled showing.

forensics.title: Friction #3: The Buyer Who Needed This Was Never Actively Found
forensics.body: At $2,350,000, this property sits in a price band where the buyer pool is selective and well-informed. Lafayette buyers at this level are comparing carefully and often shopping across multiple cities before committing to a showing. In that environment, passive MLS distribution is not enough. The buyers most likely to value a two-home compound with architectural character and hillside privacy, whether they are coming from San Francisco, Oakland, or the broader East Bay, were not being actively reached. They were waiting to be found, and the listing wasn't built to find them.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork's geo-targeted digital campaigns reach SF and East Bay buyers who are actively researching Lamorinda before they've identified a specific property, putting this compound in front of the right audience at the moment they're forming their search.

positioning_table.verdict: At $545/sqft versus a benchmark range of $780-$840/sqft, this home sits near the lower end of that range. At $545 per square foot, this compound was listed at the low end of the Lafayette fixer range, well below what even a standard renovated home in this city commands, despite offering a refreshed main residence, an architecturally distinctive ADU, hillside acreage, and no HOA. The numbers made the case for value. The strategy never made the case for what that value actually looked like. A relaunch with the right narrative and distribution has meaningful room to work with.

pillars.title: Pillar I  -  Tell the Compound Story First
pillars.body: 1603 Reliez Valley Road is not a single-family home with a bonus unit. It's a two-home compound on a hillside acre, and that's the story that leads every piece of marketing. The main home's four balconies and valley views, the ADU's architectural character and fully independent layout, and the Sport Court and outdoor living infrastructure add up to something specific and rare. Buyers looking for this kind of flexibility are a distinct audience, and they need to see it framed that way from the first image they encounter.

pillars.title: Pillar II  -  Give the ADU Its Own Visual Identity
pillars.body: An ADU attributed to Leon Meyer, with oiled redwood, walls of windows, and a remodeled primary suite, earns its own photography, its own virtual tour, and its own narrative section. Buyers can't feel the architectural character of that space from a standard listing photo. A Zillow Showcase presentation with a dedicated section for each structure, supported by immersive media, gives serious buyers the visual depth they need to understand what they're considering before they schedule a showing.

pillars.title: Pillar III  -  Reach the Buyer Who Is Still Looking
pillars.body: The buyer for this property exists. They may be in San Francisco weighing a move to the East Bay. They may be in Oakland looking for more space and privacy without leaving the region they know. They are informed, deliberate, and shopping at a price point where they can wait for the right thing. BrightWork's geo-targeted campaigns and private buyer network are built specifically to reach that buyer before they've found what they're looking for, and to put this compound in front of them at the right moment.
